claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(e) permits the Secretary of Defense to waive SAP reporting requirements and instead provide the information and the waiver justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees'.
DoD Directive 5205.07 is the governing DoD policy for special access programs and vests central management in DoD SAPCO under the Deputy Secretary of Defense.

claims.source: Inference from the structure of 10 U.S.C. 119 and DoDD 5205.07
claims.text: The allegation of a concealed legacy recovery program is, in legal terms, an allegation about a single line of the United States Code: that 10 U.S.C. 119(e) has been used to reduce congressional knowledge of a materials exploitation activity to eight members, or that the activity was never entered into the SAP system at all. Reasoning: those are the only two possibilities the statutory scheme allows.

'Waived' is a statutory term of art traceable to a single sentence: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) substitutes, for the ordinary committee report, delivery of the information and the waiver justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' Nothing in section 119 requires that this delivery be written, recorded, retained, or shared with other members.

The parallel non-DoD, non-IC statute 50 U.S.C. 3348(e) contains the same waiver test ('would adversely affect the national security', 'case-by-case basis') but a materially WEAKER carve-down: 3348(e)(2) still requires the information to go 'to the congressional oversight committees', not merely to chairs and ranking members. The eight-member floor is therefore unique to the DoD statute.

The combination that produces a genuinely invisible program is not one provision but three stacked: 119(e) removes the content from the written record; the sec. 1061 Pub. L. 114-328 sunset (eff. 31 Dec 2021) removed the annual census that would otherwise show a count; and the DoDD 5205.07 carve-out provision (see 32 CFR 117.6) removes DCSA from the contractor facility where the work is performed. Each layer is individually lawful and documented; the stack is what defeats discovery. Reasoning stated.

claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf
claims.text: VERDICT ON THE BOARD'S QUESTION: the waiver has been exercised, and the Department of Defense says so in a currently effective, publicly released instruction - but no public document identifies a single specific instance, a count, a date, a program, or any connection to unidentified anomalous phenomena. DoD Instruction 5205.11, effective 12 September 2024, paragraph 1.2.f, states verbatim: 'The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived" when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security, pursuant to Section 119 of Title 10, United States Code. Waived SAPs remain subject to congressional oversight.' This is not a hypothetical authority described in the abstract; the rest of the instruction is written around an existing population of such programs.

claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf
claims.text: THE STRONGEST SINGLE PIECE OF EVIDENCE THAT THE POPULATION IS NON-EMPTY IS A RECURRING REVIEW REQUIREMENT. DoDI 5205.11 requires that in its annual review the Special Access Program Oversight Committee - chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense - shall assess, among four listed items, '(d) All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status.' A standing annual agenda item to decide whether waived programs should REMAIN waived is only drafted if waived programs exist. This is a 2024 document, so the finding is current, not historical.

claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf
claims.text: The Department's own definition, from the DoDI 5205.11 glossary, verbatim: 'waived SAP - A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs.' And, adjacent to it: 'unacknowledged SAP - A SAP having enhanced security measures, ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information.' A waived SAP is therefore a proper subset of the unacknowledged SAPs, distinguished precisely by the exercise of the Section 119(e)(1) waiver.

claims.source: DoD Instruction 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs', 12 September 2024, cleared for public release - https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf
claims.text: Administrative plumbing specific to waived programs exists in the same instruction, which again indicates live use rather than dormant authority. Footnote 5 reads verbatim: 'CA and OA SAPCO Directors may delegate AAA for non-waived SAPs to the DoD Component's SAPCO staff. AAA for waived SAPs may be delegated to the SAPCO Deputy Director or alternate designee.' Footnote 6 reads verbatim: 'DoD SAPCO will coordinate on PARs for judicial and other federal agency personnel for waived programs.' A department does not write delegation rules and a judicial-access coordination rule for an empty set.

claims.text: THE PUBLIC TAXONOMY HAS BEEN NARROWING. DoD Directive 5205.07, 'Special Access Program Policy', was reissued effective 12 September 2024 and cancels the 1 July 2010 version. The full public text of the 2024 directive - purpose, applicability, policy, all thirteen responsibility assignments, the governance section, the complete glossary and the reference list - contains no occurrence of the words 'waived' or 'unacknowledged' at all. The directive that used to define the waived category no longer mentions it; the taxonomy now survives publicly only in the subordinate instruction, DoDI 5205.11. Anyone checking only the directive would conclude the category no longer exists.

claims.source: Report of the Commission on Protecting and Reducing Government Secrecy (the Moynihan Commission), S. Doc. 105-2, 1997, Chapter II, as mirrored by the Federation of American Scientists - https://sgp.fas.org/library/moynihan/chap2.html
claims.text: HISTORICAL CORROBORATION FROM A CONGRESSIONALLY CHARTERED COMMISSION. The Report of the Commission on Protecting and Reducing Government Secrecy (1997), Chapter II, states verbatim: 'Among black programs, further distinction is made for "waived" programs, considered to be so sensitive that they are exempt from standard reporting requirements to the Congress. The chairperson, ranking member, and, on occasion, other members and staff of relevant Congressional committees are notified only orally of the existence of these programs.' The same passage gives the surrounding population: 'There are approximately 150 DoD-approved SAPs (the exact number is classified and others have been created but not yet formally approved), down from 200 in the late 1980s, and roughly 300 SCI compartments, compared with an estimated 800 in the late 1980s.' The Commission gives no number for the waived subset. The phrase 'notified only orally' is the operationally important one: it describes a practice under which the 119(e)(2) delivery leaves no paper.

claims.source: GAO/NSIAD-93-78, 'Defense Acquisition: Oversight of Special Access Programs Has Increased', 21 December 1992 - https://www.gao.gov/assets/nsiad-93-78.pdf
claims.text: GAO HAS DESCRIBED THE WAIVER MECHANISM BUT HAS NEVER PUBLICLY REPORTED AN INSTANCE OF ITS USE. GAO/NSIAD-93-78, the unclassified summary of a classified report, describes the mechanism verbatim: 'Section 119, 10 U.S. Code, enacted in 1987, requires DOD to submit annual reports to the congressional defense committees on special access programs. Under the law, the Secretary of Defense may waive the requirement that certain information on special access programs be included in the annual report if he determines that the inclusion would adversely affect national security. However, he must provide the excluded information to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the congressional defense committees.' The report then never returns to the subject. Its findings on waivers are about a different thing entirely - 'DOD used waivers and exemptions to limit review, documentation, and reporting requirements' refers to Defense Acquisition Board reviews, competition requirements and Selected Acquisition Reports, not to Section 119(e). Do not let these two senses of 'waiver' be conflated on the board.

claims.text: WHAT SHOULD EXIST IF THE WAIVER WERE BEING USED, AND WHY NONE OF IT IS PUBLIC. Four artefacts are implied by the statute and the DoD instruction: (i) the underlying 119(a), (b) or (c) report itself, which is classified and, for (a) and (b), no longer statutorily required after 31 December 2021; (ii) the Secretary's case-by-case determination that inclusion would adversely affect national security, which 119(e)(1) requires to be made but does not require to be recorded in any publicly indexed form; (iii) the withheld information plus a written justification delivered jointly to twelve named members, which by the Moynihan Commission's account has historically been delivered orally; and (iv) the SAPOC annual review record of whether each waived program should retain that status, which is internal to the Department. None of the four is a public document class. There is no statutory requirement anywhere in Section 119 to report the NUMBER of waivers exercised, the fact that any waiver was exercised, or an aggregate count, to anyone outside those twelve seats. The absence of a public instance is therefore fully explained by the design of the mechanism and is NOT evidence of concealment beyond what the statute itself authorises.

claims.text: NO UAP-SPECIFIC EXERCISE OF THE 119(e)(1) WAIVER WAS FOUND IN ANY PUBLIC DOCUMENT. Searches across GAO's special access program series, DoD Inspector General audits and evaluations, Congressional Research Service products, and the Senate and House Armed Services Committee document sets returned no document in which a waived special access program is linked to unidentified anomalous phenomena, and no document in which any specific exercise of the Section 119(e)(1) waiver - UAP or otherwise - is identified, dated, counted or described. The DoD Inspector General's public catalogue for special access programs consists of external peer reviews and quality control reviews of the service audit agencies' SAP audit work, plus a series of entries titled only 'CLASSIFIED REPORT (Classified)'; none addresses congressional reporting under Section 119.
DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 provides that the Senior Review Group 'Reviews all waived DoD SAPs annually. Provides recommendations to the SAPOC concerning continued waived status.'
DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 provides that the SRG 'Ensures the accuracy of the SAP list submitted to Congress prior to submission of the SAP annual report.'
DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 2 requires DoD SAPCO to establish 'the criteria for annual reviews of waived DoD SAPs by the SSWG and SRG.'

DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.f limits access to waived SAPs, absent SecDef or DepSecDef approval, to 'the chair, the ranking minority member, and the staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees'.

A complete list of waived DoD SAPs demonstrably exists in documentary form, is reviewed at least annually by the Senior Review Group, and is validated by the SAPOC - which means the answer to 'how many waived programs are there' is a retrievable agency record and not an unknowable. Reasoning: DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 assigns the annual review of all waived SAPs and the accuracy of the congressional SAP list to a named standing body.

desc: A waived unacknowledged special access program is the most protected category of activity the United States government operates. Special access programs are activities requiring protection beyond that ordinarily required for information at the same classification level, imposing need-to-know controls, access rosters and separate security architecture; DoD Directive 5205.07 governs them. An unacknowledged SAP is one whose existence is not acknowledged - the response to an inquiry is neither confirmation nor denial. A waived SAP is one for which the Secretary of Defense has exercised the waiver at 10 U.S.C. 119(e), under which the annual report and the justification for the waiver go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' instead of to the committees as a whole. Combine the two and the result is an activity whose existence is denied to the public, denied to most of Congress, and known in the legislative branch to eight people. Every serious allegation on this board reduces to a claim about this category: David Grusch's testimony that a multi-decade materials recovery and exploitation effort exists and is unreported; the 2009 Reid request that AAWSAP be granted restricted SAP status, which USD(I) James Clapper opposed; the 2011 DHS attempt to stand up KONA BLUE as a prospective SAP; and the FY2024 NDAA section 1687 limitation on the use of funds for UAP-related programs not reported to the congressional defense committees, which is Congress legislating directly against the possibility that this category has been abused.

claims.text: Department of Defense training doctrine defines the category: 'Under extremely limited circumstances, unacknowledged SAPs may also be waived. Waived SAPs are unacknowledged SAPs for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting requirements under Section 119, Title 10 U.S. Code. Waived SAPs have more restrictive reporting requirements and access controls.'

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1): 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.'

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) requires that when the waiver authority is exercised, the withheld information and the justification for the waiver be provided 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) provides: "The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis."

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) provides that when the waiver authority is exercised, the Secretary shall provide the withheld information and the justification for the waiver "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees" — and 119(g) defines the defense committees as the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees plus the defense appropriations subcommittees of both chambers, i.e. six bodies and twelve members.

10 U.S.C. 119(b)(2)(B) requires each new-SAP report to include "an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program that is the subject of the notice" — a comparative-technology disclosure that a 119(e) waiver can remove.
10 U.S.C. 119(f) prohibits initiating a special access program until the defense committees are notified and 30 days elapse after notification.

The annual reporting requirements of 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b) terminated effective December 31, 2021, pursuant to section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328, as recorded in the Termination of Reporting Requirements note to section 119.

DoD Instruction 5205.11, September 12, 2024, paragraph 1.2.f states: "The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as 'waived' when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security, pursuant to Section 119 of Title 10, United States Code. Waived SAPs remain subject to congressional oversight."

DoDI 5205.11 defines a waived SAP as "A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs."

DoDI 5205.11 defines an unacknowledged SAP as "A SAP having enhanced security measures, ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information."

DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.a(3) states: "Only the chair, the ranking member, the staff directors, and one designated security manager of the defense and intelligence committees will be authorized access to waived DoD SAPs within their committee's respective oversight jurisdiction. Requests to access additional members of Congress or professional staff must be approved by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense."

DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.a(2) provides that access to a SAP umbrella conveys access to all subordinate compartments and sub-compartments "with the exception of waived sub-compartments" — meaning a waived sub-compartment can sit inside a program a member has otherwise been read into.

DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.c(1) limits committee professional staff access to non-waived SAPs only, and paragraph 7.2.f states flatly: "The personal staff of a member of Congress will not be granted access to DoD SAPs."

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) is the statutory Gang of Eight provision: where the President determines it essential to limit access to a covert action finding, the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House, and the majority and minority leaders of the Senate.

50 U.S.C. 3093(e) defines covert action as activity "to influence political, economic, or military conditions abroad" and expressly excludes "traditional counterintelligence activities, traditional activities to improve or maintain the operational security of United States Government programs, or administrative activities" and "traditional diplomatic or military activities or routine support to such activities" — so a domestic material recovery, custody and exploitation effort would generate no Presidential finding and no reporting obligation under section 3093 at all.

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) requires that not later than 180 days after a limited-access statement of reasons is submitted, the President either give all members of the intelligence committees access to the finding or submit a renewed statement of reasons for continued limitation — a sunset discipline that has no counterpart in 10 U.S.C. 119(e).

dossier.denialPosture: There is no denial to catalogue, because the Department has never publicly acknowledged any individual waived SAP; acknowledging one would defeat the category. What is on the record instead is a quieter act: the September 12, 2024 reissuance of DoD Directive 5205.07 removed the acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived taxonomy from the public policy document entirely, while DoD's own unclassified training material continues to teach it. The public governing directive no longer names the category by which programs are lawfully hidden from Congress.
dossier.narrative:
The architecture has four layers, and each one narrows the audience.

Layer one is the baseline reporting duty. 10 U.S.C. 119, added by Public Law 100-180 section 1132(a)(1) on December 4, 1987, required the Secretary of Defense to submit to the defense committees an annual report on special access programs by March 1 of each year, setting out the total amount requested for SAPs in the President's budget and, for each SAP, a brief description, its major milestones, its actual cost for each prior fiscal year, and its estimated total cost across the current year, the budget year and four succeeding years. Subsection (b) required a separate annual report by February 1 giving notice and justification for each new SAP designation, with the current total program cost estimate and an identification of existing programs or technologies similar in technology or mission to the one being hidden. Subsection (f), added by Public Law 101-510 section 1482(a)(2) in November 1990, added the hard gate: a special access program may not be initiated until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse.

Layer two is the waiver. Subsection (e)(1) provides that the Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security, with each waiver made on a case-by-case basis. Subsection (e)(2) then routes the withheld information and the justification jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees. Steven Aftergood of the Federation of American Scientists put the practical result plainly: waived SAPs are exempted by statute (10 USC 119e) from normal congressional notification requirements, and in such cases only eight senior members of the congressional defense committees may be advised of the program.

Layer three is DoD policy, which is more restrictive than the statute. Under the pre-2024 SAP policy framework, only the chair, the ranking minority member and the staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees are authorized access to waived DoD SAPs within their committee's oversight role, absent approval by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary. The currently effective directive, DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued September 12, 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks, adds a provision that is the operational choke point for whistleblowers: no DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval. The people most likely to hold the evidence are contractors, and the directive forbids them from handing it to Congress without permission from the office that runs the SAP system.

Layer four is the quiet erosion of the reporting baseline itself. The U.S. Code note under section 119 records that for termination, effective December 31, 2021, of the provisions in subsections (a) and (b) requiring submittal of an annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Public Law 114-328. The annual SAP report and the annual new-SAP notification report, the two instruments the 1987 Congress built, were sunset by a general reporting-requirement cull. And the September 12, 2024 reissuance of DoDD 5205.07 does not define waived SAP anywhere in its glossary. It defines SAP, SAP architecture, SAP umbrella, SAP compartment, SAP sub-compartment, Joint Force Integration SAP and Strategic Enabler SAP. The acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived taxonomy that appears in DoD's own training material has been replaced in the public directive by a vocabulary that does not distinguish between programs Congress is told about and programs it is not. Whether that is reform or relabeling, the public governing document no longer names the category.

The rest of the directive maps the custody chain. All DoD SAPs are assigned to an oversight authority drawn from USD(R&E), USD(A&S), USD(P), USD(I&S) and the Director of the DoD SAP Central Office. The Director of DoD SAPCO reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense, holds delegated Top Secret original classification authority for all DoD SAP information, publishes and maintains the security classification guides for every SAP umbrella, accredits congressional SAP facilities, and maintains records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress. Establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments is by exception and requires Secretary or Deputy Secretary approval. The senior governing body, the SAP Oversight Committee, is chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense. Approximately 75 to 80 per cent of all DoD SAPs are acquisition SAPs, which is the category that would cover a materials exploitation or reverse-engineering effort.

Congress has attacked the funding side rather than the classification side. FY2024 NDAA section 1687(b) makes independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena unallowable as an indirect expense on covered contracts unless the material and information is made available to the congressional defense committees, both intelligence committees, and the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and the Speaker and minority leader of the House. That is an admission on the face of the statute that Congress believed UAP work was being charged to the taxpayer through contractor overhead and reported to no one. It is also a route around the waiver, because IR&D allowability is an accounting question, not a classification question.

dossier.whatItIs: A waived unacknowledged special access program is the most tightly held category in the Department of Defense classification system. Department of Defense training doctrine defines it in one sentence: 'Waived SAPs are unacknowledged SAPs for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting requirements under Section 119, Title 10 U.S. Code.' The waiver authority is 10 U.S.C. 119(e), under which the Secretary may withhold specified information from the statutory reports to Congress if he determines that including it would adversely affect national security, and must then provide the information and the justification for the waiver only to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the mechanism. If a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering program exists and has been concealed from Congress, waived SAP status is the lawful instrument by which that concealment is accomplished, and no unlawful act is required to sustain it. The statute permits an entire program's existence, cost, milestones and technology to disappear from the reports Congress wrote to keep itself informed, on the unilateral written determination of a single official. The population read in on the legislative side collapses to twelve members and, per DoD policy, their staff directors. Everyone else in Congress, including every member of both intelligence committees who is not chair or ranking, can hold a Top Secret clearance and still be told nothing exists. The system is designed to produce truthful denials from officials who genuinely do not know, which is the precise pathology alleged across every UAP whistleblower account since 2017.

entityInfo.desc: Terms of art, precisely. A special access program imposes protection beyond that required for information at the same classification level - access rosters, separate billets, dedicated security architecture. An ACKNOWLEDGED SAP appears in the budget by name with a classified purpose. An UNACKNOWLEDGED SAP is one whose existence is not confirmed; the correct response to an inquiry is neither confirmation nor denial. A WAIVED unacknowledged SAP adds the 10 U.S.C. 119(e) waiver, which removes the program from the report to the defense committees and substitutes notification to the chairman and ranking member of each. Every substantive allegation on this board resolves into one of exactly two propositions: that a materials acquisition and exploitation activity exists as a waived USAP known to eight members of Congress, or that it exists outside the SAP system entirely and is therefore unlawful. The first is testable by demanding the waived-SAP list. The second is testable by an ISOO NISP audit of cleared facilities. Neither test has been run.
